Predict a fitted model onto a regular grid

Source: R/predict-surface.R
predict_surface.Rd

Builds a prediction surface over the extent of the training data (or over a grid you supply), predicts in chunks, and returns an sf layer.

Usage

predict_surface(
  object,
  grid = NULL,
  cell_size = NULL,
  n_cells = 10000L,
  boundary = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  chunk_size = 5000L,
  se = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A spatial_fit (from fit_rf_model(), fit_gwr_model() or fit_bayesian_spatial_model()).

grid

Optional sf POINT layer to predict onto, with at least one row. When NULL, a regular grid is built over the training extent. A grid of polygons is reduced to points; see "Coordinate reference systems and geometry".

cell_size

Grid resolution in CRS units. Ignored when grid is supplied; when NULL, derived from n_cells. A value that would produce more than 5,000,000 cells is refused, naming the implied count and the CRS units. The usual cause is a value in the wrong unit. The grid is centred on the training bounding box and covers it: when the extent is not a whole number of cells, it overhangs the box by less than one cell, split evenly between the two sides. A cell_size wider than the extent yields a single centred cell.

n_cells

Approximate cell count used to derive cell_size. Default 10000. Must be a single positive finite number and at most 5,000,000; anything else is an error. Also ignored when grid is supplied. The grid you pass is used verbatim.

boundary

Optional polygonal sf/sfc; grid points outside it are dropped. Aligned to the fit's CRS as grid is.

covariates

Optional sf layer carrying the model's predictors. Required when the model has predictors and grid does not already contain them. Values are taken from the nearest feature (see "Ties between nearest covariate features"). Aligned to the fit's CRS as grid is, with the same warning when it has no CRS.

chunk_size

Rows per prediction call. Default 5000. A performance setting only: rows do not interact, and for a bayesian_fit the GP boundary is held at its fitted value whatever the chunk holds (see spatial_fit-predict). The two warnings in which predict() on a GWR fit counts locations (classes "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation" and "spatialkit_gwr_not_estimable") are raised once for the grid, with its totals, whatever the number of chunks.

se

Logical; also return a standard error (or posterior SD) column where the backend supports it. Default FALSE. For a bayesian_fit this is the SD of the posterior draws predict() returns, and those are of the expected value by default (type = "epred"): the uncertainty of the mean surface, not of a new observation, which also carries the observation noise. For the predictive SD, the one that goes with prediction intervals and cv_bayes()'s calibration, pass type = "predict" as well.

...

Passed to predict(), e.g. type = "predict" for a bayesian_fit. Not draws, which this function sets itself and refuses here.

Value

An sf POINT layer with a .pred column, and .pred_se when se = TRUE and the backend gives one. A .pred_se column that a supplied grid carries from an earlier surface is removed when this call adds none. For an auto-generated grid the resolution is attached as attribute "cell_size". For a user-supplied grid it is only whatever "cell_size" attribute that object already carried. That is usually NULL, and NULL for certain if the grid had to be re-projected, since st_transform() does not preserve custom attributes.

Details

predict_surface() builds the grid, joins the covariates, aligns the CRSs and calls predict() in chunks of chunk_size rows. Rows do not interact, so chunking changes memory use and not the predictions. For a bayesian_fit the draw matrix is n_draws by the number of rows, which on a fine grid outgrows memory long before the fit does.

Coordinate reference systems and geometry

grid, boundary and covariates are brought into the fit's CRS first. A layer without a CRS is read the way the training data were (the assumption recorded on the fit), with a warning, and then reprojected; when that reading is longitude and latitude, a layer with an x outside -180 to 360 or a y beyond 90 north or south cannot be in it, and the call stops. Without this a CRS-less grid could land thousands of kilometres from the covariates, and every cell would take the same nearest feature. A layer still without a CRS after that is taken as EPSG:4326 and reprojected when its coordinates look like longitude and latitude, and otherwise stamped with the fit's CRS, with a warning either way; a fit's CRS in longitude and latitude is not stamped on coordinates outside longitude -180 to 360 and latitude -90 to 90, which is refused. See spatialkit-geometry for these rules in general.

A grid of polygons (create_grid_polygons() output, say) is reduced to one representative point per cell, as coerce_to_points() does, so covariates are taken at the location predicted for; boundary then keeps the cells whose point falls inside it. All three layers are read in x and y: one whose geometries mix XY with XYZ or XYM, or carry M (XYM or XYZM), is read without its Z and M, with no warning for a boundary or covariates. A POINT grid whose coordinates are not moved (one in the fit's CRS, or one without a CRS that is stamped with it) is returned with its rows as given, Z and M included; one that mixes dimensions and is reprojected into the fit's CRS comes back in XY with a warning of class "spatialkit_zm_dropped". The points a grid of polygons is reduced to are in XY when its geometries mix dimensions or carry M.

A grid row without a location (an empty geometry, or a coordinate that is not finite or lies beyond 1e150) gets an NA prediction; in a grid that is reprojected, or reduced from polygons, it comes back as an empty point. A covariate row without a location is never the nearest feature.

Ties between nearest covariate features

A grid point the same distance from several features of covariates takes one of them by a fixed rule, so a grid laid between the points of a lattice takes the same covariates in another unit or with another origin, and with or without the FNN package.

  • Points. Distances count as equal when the squared distance is no more than the square of the least distance lengthened by a margin, plus one part in ten million of the least squared distance. Among them the point lowest in x is taken, then the one lowest in y, then the first in row order. x values count as one when they lie within one part in ten million of the diagonal of the points' bounding box, or within the margin where that is more; y values are read the same way. A grid point near two points that lie within the margin of each other (two records of one station that differ only in the last bits of their coordinates) takes the same one however near it lies.

  • Lines and polygons, or a layer that mixes them with points (on the edge two polygons share, say). Distances within one part in ten million of the least, plus the margin, count as the same. Among them the feature whose bounding-box centre is lowest in x is taken, then lowest in y, x values and y values within one part in ten million of the diagonal of the bounding box of covariates counting as one, then the first in row order.

  • A layer in degrees. The nearest feature is sf::st_nearest_feature()'s, which settles a tie in the order its search meets the features (GEOS, or s2 while sf::sf_use_s2() is on).

  • The margin. It is one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the features that have a location, at most a millionth of the diagonal of their bounding box and at least four times the spacing of doubles at that coordinate. It grows with the largest coordinate: about 0.46 mm at a UTM northing near 4,550 km, about half a micrometre once the origin lies next to data 5 km across. So a grid point whose distances to two features differ by less than the margin with one origin and by more with another takes the one the tie rule picks with the first and the nearer with the second.

See also

area_of_applicability() to mark where the surface applies, and spatial_fit-predict for the predictions of each backend.

Other prediction: area_of_applicability(), plot.aoa(), print.aoa()

Examples

# Any spatial_fit works here; a forest keeps the example free of the
# optional GWR and Stan backends.
library(sf)
set.seed(1)
n <- 120
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
             elev = rnorm(n)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
pts$price <- 10 + 0.01 * (st_coordinates(pts)[, 1] - 5e5) +
  2 * pts$elev + rnorm(n)
fit  <- fit_rf_model(pts, "price", "elev", num_trees = 100, seed = 1)
surf <- predict_surface(fit, n_cells = 500, covariates = pts)
surf[".pred"]               # one prediction per grid cell, as an sf layer
#> Simple feature collection with 529 features and 1 field
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 500026.7 ymin: 5000038 xmax: 500979 ymax: 5000990
#> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N
#> First 10 features:
#>       .pred                 geometry
#> 1  11.53496 POINT (500026.7 5000038)
#> 2  11.71447   POINT (500070 5000038)
#> 3  11.71447 POINT (500113.3 5000038)
#> 4  12.06628 POINT (500156.6 5000038)
#> 5  12.06628 POINT (500199.9 5000038)
#> 6  12.06628 POINT (500243.2 5000038)
#> 7  13.07745 POINT (500286.5 5000038)
#> 8  13.07745 POINT (500329.7 5000038)
#> 9  13.07745   POINT (500373 5000038)
#> 10 11.63669 POINT (500416.3 5000038)
# Check where the surface extrapolates before mapping it.  The grid took
# its covariates from the nearest observation, so here nothing is
# outside; covariates from another source, such as a raster converted to
# sf points, are where this bites.
area_of_applicability(surf, model = fit)
#> Area of applicability (Meyer & Pebesma 2021)
#> 
#>   predictors  : 1 (elev)
#>   weighted    : yes, by the model's permutation importance, floored at 0
#>   training    : 120 points
#>   reference   : nearest other training point (no folds supplied)
#>   normaliser  : 1.1283 (mean pairwise distance)
#>   threshold   : 0.0480 (outlier-removed max of training DI)
#>   location    : not measured
#> 
#>   529 of 529 prediction points inside the AOA (100.0%)
